case_name: Lund v. Black Press Group Ltd.
text:
IN THE SUPREME
COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

Lund v. Black Press Group Ltd.,

2007 BCSC 559

Date: 20070426

Docket:
05/0964

Registry: Victoria

Between:

Erik
Lund

Plaintiff

And:

Black
Press Group Ltd., Island Publishers Limited,

Rod Sluggett, Robin Wark, Shannon Moneo,

Victor Wehmann, Michael Thornton and Merell Harlow

Defendants

Before:
The Honourable Mr. Justice Metzger

Reasons for Judgment

Counsel for the Plaintiff

D. D. McKnight

Counsel for the
Defendants, Michael Thornton, Victor Wehmann and Merell Harlow

R.
D. McConchie

Date and Place of Trial/Hearing:

February
22, 2007

Victoria,
B.C.

[
1
]

The plaintiff, Erik Lund, was the Regional
Director for the Juan de Fuca Electoral Area of the Capital Regional District
of B.C. when, he alleges, the defendants wrote or published defamatory
statements about him.  On the application before the court, defendants Victor Wehmann,
Michael Thornton and Merell Harlow (the “Defendants”) ask the court to:

1.   strike select subparagraphs of the Statement of Claim pursuant
to Rule 19(24) of the
Rules of Court
;

2.   alternatively, grant the Defendants leave to set down a
pre-trial hearing pursuant to Rule 34;

3.   strike paragraph 32 of the Statement of Claim on the ground
that the plaintiff has failed to state particulars of special damages as
required by Rule 19(11) or on the ground that the plaintiff has failed to plead
further particulars of special damages as required by Rule 19(11.1);

4.   alternatively, order the plaintiff to deliver particulars of
special damages, within 10 days pursuant to Rule 19(16), that includes the
amount of the loss, the date(s) when the loss was incurred, the names of the
customers involved and which losses were caused by each publication complained
of in the Statement of Claim.

Rules
19(24) and 34

[
2
]

Although the Defendants seek relief on the basis
of Rule 19(24)(a)-(d), I find that Rule 19(24)(a) is most applicable.  It reads
as follows:

(24)     At any stage
of a proceeding the court may order to be struck out or amended the whole or
any part of an endorsement, pleading, petition or other document on the ground
that

(a)       it
discloses no reasonable claim or defence as the case may be,…

and the court may grant judgment or order
the proceeding to be stayed or dismissed...

[
3
]

In
Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v.
Canadian Jewish Congress
(1999),
1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
,
36 C.P.C. (4
th
) 266
, [1999] B.C.J. No. 2160 (B.C.S.C.) at para.

34
, Romilly J. provides a concise summary of what is required to succeed on an
application under Rule 19(24):

To succeed on an
application under Rule 19(24)(a) it must be established that it is "plain
and obvious" that the pleading discloses no reasonable cause of action:
Hunt v. Carey,
1990 CanLII 90 (SCC)
, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 959 (S.C.C.).  If there is any doubt it should
be resolved in the favour of permitting the pleadings to stand: McGauley v.
British Columbia (1989),
1989 CanLII 2809 (BC CA)
, 39 B.C.L.R. (2d) 223 (B.C.C.A.).  The court should
proceed on the assumption that all facts pled are true:  Helman v. Brown
(1966),
1966 CanLII 597 (BC CA)
, 57 W.W.R. 608 (B.C.C.A.).  The only question then is whether the facts
disclose a cause of action: Minnes v. Minnes (1962),
1962 CanLII 350 (BC CA)
, 39 W.W.R. 112 (B.C.C.A.); McNaughten
v. Baker (1988),
1988 CanLII 3036 (BC CA)
, 25 B.C.L.R. (2d) 17 (C.A.).  In other words, as long as the
pleadings disclose a triable issue, either as it exists, or as it may be
amended, then the issue should go to trial.  The mere fact that the case is
weak or not likely to succeed is no ground for striking it out under the
provisions of Rule 19(24): Minnes, supra.

[
4
]

In determining whether it is plain and obvious
that defamation pleadings disclose a reasonable cause of action, the court will
assess whether the words complained of are reasonably capable of bearing the
meanings alleged.  In making such an assessment, the court will determine
whether reasonable persons of ordinary intelligence would read the words
complained of as lowering the plaintiff in the estimation of right thinking
members of society and cause him to be regarded with feelings of hatred,
contempt, ridicule, fear, dislike or disesteem (see
Sturdy v. Canada
(Minister of National Defence)
,

2005 BCSC 519
).

[
5
]

In the case at bar, the Defendants seek only to
strike select alleged meanings, not the entire defamation claims against them.  Although
I was unable to find a B.C. case where a court essentially pruned the pleadings
in a defamation action, in my opinion there is sufficient authority for doing
so.  First, Rule 19(24) states that a court may strike out or amend the whole
or
any part
of a pleading.  I am satisfied that the Rule provides authority to
cull pleadings without striking the entire claim.  Indeed, under Rule 19(24),
the court struck out only select phrases and paragraphs of a statement of
defence (see
Hemming v. Newton
,
2006 BCSC 1748
).

[
6
]

Second, the object of the
Rules of Court
,
as expressed in Rule 1(5) is to “secure the just, speedy and inexpensive
determination of every proceeding on its merits”.  If the words complained of
in a defamation action are not reasonably capable of bearing some of the
meanings that are alleged, it would be efficient and just for the court to
strike those alleged meanings.

[
7
]

During submissions, counsel for the plaintiff
explained that he did not come prepared to argue whether or not the Defendants’
statements are capable of bearing the meanings alleged.  The plaintiff submits
that I must proceed on the premise that every fact alleged in the Statement of
Claim is true.  In particular, the plaintiff submits that the inferential
meanings alleged must be presumed to be true.  It is the plaintiff’s position
that whether words are capable of bearing the meanings alleged is more properly
argued under Rule 34.  The plaintiff submits that the most the court can do, on
this application, is to order that certain statements and their alleged
meanings be set down for further argument on whether the words are capable of
bearing the meanings alleged.

[
8
]

I do not agree with the plaintiff’s submissions.
Whether words are capable of a defamatory meaning is a question of law (
Lions
Gate Marketing Company Ltd. v. Used Car Dealers Association of Ontario
,

2005 BCCA 274
at para.
11
).  Whether words actually mean what is alleged is a
question of fact.  The only way that I can determine whether to strike any part
of the pleadings in a defamation case, pursuant to Rule 19(24), is to assess
whether or not the words are capable of supporting the meanings alleged.  If I
find, from the perspective of a reasonable person of ordinary intelligence,
that the words are not capable of supporting the meanings alleged, I can strike
them pursuant to Rule 19(24) and do not have to set the matter over for
consideration under Rule 34.  In deciding whether a plaintiff has disclosed a
reasonable cause of action, I must examine the legal basis for his claim.  In
defamation, this involves assessing whether the allegedly defamatory words are
capable of supporting the meanings which are claimed.

[
9
]

I will analyze the pleadings according to the
statements made and meanings alleged by each of the Defendants.

Defendant Wehmann

[
10
]

Paragraphs 16 and 17 contain the first
statements and alleged meanings made by Defendant Wehmann.  They read as
follows:

16.       In or about June of 2003, the Defendant Wehmann wrote to
the Defendant Black Press and, or alternatively, the Defendant Island
Publishers, and on June 18, 2003, said Defendants printed and published in Sooke
News Mirror a letter which read, in part, as follows:

"           At a community meeting in
East Sooke June 9 Director Lund stated that he was always 'uneasy' about two
directors deciding land use matters and under his proposal there would be three
directors.
It is a matter of conjecture whether Director Lund didn't think
or doesn't understand the old and new systems or he was intentionally
misleading the public at this meeting.

In fact, the two
directors of the old electoral areas would second each other's motions at the
CRD Board and all 22 directors voted on those motions.  Under the procedural
bylaw of the CRD board a show of hands is not required to vote in the
affirmative.  Under the system of a single director, a seconder of his/her
motion must be found.  This was the beginning of the problems for the CRD board
to deal with land use matters in the new JDF electoral area.  The Order in
Council that Director Lund wishes to amend, took away the voting rights of 14
of the 22 CRD Directors that voted on land use in the past.  Now, in our area,
we have a five member committee chaired by Director Lund.

As you can see the
direct involvement by the CRD Board was reduced by nearly two-thirds.
Mr.
Lund wants to consolidate his own personal power
by further reduction in
the size of the Land Use Committees.
It makes one wonder if the seeking of
consensus on a committee of five is being sacrificed for the sake of expediency
and perhaps personal agenda.

Land use issues can be
divisive and contentious as we all know, but we have a process, which includes
elected APCs and public hearings.  Those are the venues to express our opinions
to a broad base, experienced five member Land Use Committee.
This process
ensures that all of us are heard and listened to, not only those that supported
one particular politician during his or her election campaign
."          [emphasis
added]

17.       The statements contained in paragraph 16 herein are
defamatory in their natural and ordinary meaning and the innuendoes contained
therein in that they mean or were understood to mean that:

a.         the Plaintiff is
uninformed about matters concerning his public office and makes important
decisions without sufficient deliberation;

b.         in discharging his
official duties, the Plaintiff is actuated by self-interest to the detriment of
the public that he was elected to serve;

c.         the Plaintiff improperly
exercised his influence as a public official in favour of persons who supported
his political campaign.

[
11
]

The Defendant Wehmann submits that nothing in
paragraph 16 is capable of bearing the meanings alleged in 17 a. and 17 c.  I
agree.  The only part of Defendant Wehmann’s writing that makes reference to
the plaintiff’s knowledge or deliberation is the first underlined portion in
paragraph 16.  Rather than state that the plaintiff does not think or is
unaware, the Defendant Wehmann writes that it is a matter of “conjecture”.  In
my view, a reasonable person of ordinary intelligence would understand
Defendant Wehmann as providing possible rationales, in the form of conjecture,
for Director Lund’s statement at the community meeting not definitive
statements about him that would lower him in the eyes of the community or cause
him to be regarded with hatred, contempt, ridicule, fear, dislike or disesteem.

[
12
]

Similarly, I am unable
to find that anything in paragraph 16 is capable of meaning that the plaintiff
improperly exercised his influence as a public official in favour of persons
who supported his political campaign.  Nowhere in paragraph 16 does it say that
the plaintiff improperly exercised his influence.  Defendant Wehmann writes
that “Mr. Lund wants to consolidate his own personal power”.  This does not
mean that he has consolidated personal power or that a desire to do so is an
improper exercise of influence.  The Defendant Wehmann further states that one
wonders whether the “seeking of consensus on a committee of five is being
sacrificed for the sake of expedience and perhaps personal agenda”.  This
statement is similarly prospective and speculative and does not mean that the
plaintiff has improperly exercised his influence.

[
13
]

Further, neither of
these two statements say or imply that the plaintiff’s desire to consolidate
personal power or his personal agenda are connected to persons who supported
the plaintiff in his political campaign.  The only reference to the plaintiff’s
election campaign is in the last underlined portion of paragraph 16.  In my
view, a reasonable person of ordinary intelligence would understand the
Defendant Wehmann as saying that several elected people making land use decisions
ensures that a greater proportion of the public is heard than if only Mr. Lund
makes decisions as he would most represent the views of that segment of the
population that voted for him.  In my view, nothing in paragraph 16 supports
the meaning alleged in 17 c.

[
14
]

Paragraphs 18 and 19 of
the Statement of Claim contain the second statement and alleged meanings made
by the Defendant Wehmann:

18.       In or about July of 2003, the
Defendant Wehmann wrote to the Defendant Black Press and, or alternatively, the
Defendant Island Publishers, and on July 2, 2003, said Defendants printed and
published in Sooke News Mirror a letter which read, in part, as follows:

"           It appears that most of
the reasons Director Lund stated May 28 to the CRD Board and later in his
'public meetings' to support his request for a change in the voting structure,
have suddenly lost their validity.

Many of us attended
Director Lund's meetings in order to have input and voice our opinions on a
motion that he later withdrew from the board, two days before the board's
regular meeting.

It is an insult to the
electorate and a mockery of our public process when an elected official
pretends to seek the public's input on a motion before this board and then
withdraws that motion to substitute it with an entirely different motion to
that board.  A motion that was never presented for public debate.  This is
Lund's third version in as many weeks.  His new motion seeks the removal of
Langford and Colwood, two of our closest neighbours along with Metchosin, and replaces
them with Highlands and Central Saanich.  It seems that Lund is getting further
and further away from our areas to try and stack LUC 'A' in his favour.  Why
should a couple of mayors living each of the Trans-Canada Highway have any say
in our decisions out here!

The last minute switch
by Director Lund undermines the public's trust and faith in due process and
ignores the board's instruction to Director Lund in regard to seeking public
input.  Obviously the CRD chair and board had a problem with Director Lund's
manipulations and pulled his agenda item at last Wednesday's meeting.

The CRD Board set up
the existing committees after much debate and valid reasoning.  Those reasons
have not change, only the director of the electoral area has.  Perhaps if Lund
had been more honest and forthright during his election campaign as to his true
agenda, he could have saved himself a lot of embarrassment."

19.       The statements contained in paragraph 18 herein are
defamatory in their natural and ordinary meaning and the innuendoes contained
therein in that they mean or were understood to mean that:

a.         the Plaintiff
conducted himself arbitrarily and capriciously in his capacity as a public
official;

b.         the Plaintiff is a
liar;

c.         in discharging his
official duties, the Plaintiff is actuated by self-interest to the detriment of
the public that he was elected to serve;

d.         the Plaintiff acted
insubordinately and contrary to the direction of his superiors in the discharge
of his official duties;

e.         the Plaintiff has committed a
breach of trust in his capacity of public official, contrary to
section 122
of
the
Criminal Code of Canada
.

[
15
]

The Defendant Wehmann submits that his writing,
as expressed in paragraph 18, is not capable of bearing the alleged meaning in
paragraph 19 e.
Section 122
of the
Criminal Code
states:

Every official
who, in connection with the duties of his office, commits fraud or a breach of
trust is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to imprisonment for a term
not exceeding five years, whether or not the fraud or breach of trust would be
an offence if it were committed in relation to private persons.

[
16
]

Defendant Wehmann takes issue with the
plaintiff’s approach to seeking public input on motions before the board.  No
reasonable person of ordinary intelligence would understand the Defendant Wehmann
to be saying that because the plaintiff has curtailed public debate and input
that he has committed fraud or breach of trust while in office such that he
should be charged criminally.  The Defendant Wehmann’s statements do not even
come close to supporting such a meaning.

[
17
]

In summary, in relation
to Defendant Wehmann, I strike a and c from paragraph 17, as well as e from
paragraph 19.

Defendant Thornton

[
18
]

The plaintiff alleges that the Defendant
Thornton made defamatory statements about him on three different occasions.  The
first of these is found at paragraphs 20 and 21 of the Statement of Claim:

20.       In or about June or July of
2003, the Defendant Thornton wrote to the Defendant Black Press and, or alternatively,
the Defendant Island Publishers, and on July 2, 2003, said Defendants printed
and published in Sooke News Mirror a letter which read, in part, as follows:

"           Friends and neighbours,
beware.  I believe regional director Erik Lund has devious plans afoot.

Why else would the man
opposed to elected Advisory Planning Commissions keep trying to alter the
voting rights on our Juan de Fuca Electoral Area Land Use Committee 'A'?

First he wants a
weighted vote.  Then he wants total control with he and Metchosin having two of
three votes.  When that doesn't fly, he proposes replaces directors from
neighbouring Colwood and Langford with far away Highlands and Central Saanich.

The fact pattern
suggests that Director Lund wants to make radical land use changes, which he
has not yet publicly disclosed, and that he knows will not be supported by the
current majority of Committee 'A'.

While he seeks these
changes Director Lund has convened a new local area planning group, dominated
by those who previously supported stripping property owners of their rights.

Through amendments to
the community plan, unsuspecting families on Galliano Island lost their
historic right to build even a single-family home, unless they now give away 75
per cent of their land.

If you don't think it
can happen here, just remember how quickly former Regional Director Diane
Bernard down-zoned 14,000 acres of electoral area land, massively devaluing
property owned by longtime residents and honest taxpayers.  To escape such
draconian dictatorship, Sooke incorporated and immediately restored property
rights.  The rest of us were fortunate Brain (sic) Henson defeated Bernard in
the subsequent election and restored our property rights as well.

Now we must survive
Erik Lund.  Do any of us really need more of the pain, anguish, conflict and
economic misery he can create all across our communities if he's allowed to rig
the voting procedure?"

21.       The statements contained in paragraph 20 herein are
defamatory in their natural and ordinary meaning and the innuendoes contained
therein in that they mean or were understood to mean that:

a.         the Plaintiff
deceitfully used or attempted to use the powers of his office to manipulate the
decision-making process relating to land use issues;

b.         the Plaintiff has
caused personal and economic strife for the public that he was elected to
serve;

c.         the Plaintiff is unfit to serve
in public office.

[
19
]

The Defendant Thornton submits that nothing in
paragraph 20 is capable of supporting the meanings alleged in paragraph 21 b and
c.  I agree.  There is nothing in paragraph 20 that could mean that the
plaintiff has caused personal and economic strife for the public he was elected
to serve.  The article begins by alerting friends and neighbours to “devious
plans afoot”.  This suggests that any personal or economic strife has yet to
occur.  The Defendant Thornton then refers to rights lost by families on Galiano
Island, and how a former regional director down-zoned 14,000 acres of electoral
land.  Neither of these situations, and the personal and economic strike they
may have caused, had anything to do with the plaintiff.  The Defendant Thornton
then asks if anyone needs “more of the pain, anguish, conflict and economic
misery” that the plaintiff “can” create “if” he’s allowed to rig the vote.  This
statement is not capable of bearing the meaning that the plaintiff has caused
personal and economic strife as it is prospective in nature.  This statement
merely warns the public of what may come to pass, not what has occurred.

[
20
]

Similarly, I am unable
to find anything in paragraph 20 that suggests that the plaintiff is unfit to
serve in public office.  The Defendant Thornton takes issue with the
plaintiff’s alleged attempts and desires to alter the voting rights in the Juan
de Fuca Electoral Area Land Use Committee.  Defendant Thornton then lists the
alleged steps the plaintiff has taken to change the voting procedures so that
the Regional Director for the Juan de Fuca Electoral Area has greater control.  Although
Defendant Thornton clearly does not agree with this political manoeuvring, he
does not say or suggest that the plaintiff is unfit to serve in public office.  The
alleged fact that the plaintiff wants to make radical land use changes does not
mean that he is unfit.  A reasonable person of ordinary intelligence would not
understand Defendant Thornton to be saying that the plaintiff is unfit to serve
in public office, but rather that the Defendant Thornton does not agree with
the plaintiff’s political decisions and manoeuvring.

[
21
]

The next allegedly
defamatory statement by Defendant Thornton is found at paragraphs 22 and 23 of
the Statement of Claim:

22.       In an issue of the Times
Colonist, a newspaper circulated on Vancouver Island and throughout the
province of British Columbia, printed July 16, 2003, there was falsely and
maliciously published of and concerning the Plaintiff an article that stated,
among other things, the following:

“           Thornton said no new map was
submitted.  Even committee member and Langford Coun. Lanny Seaton argues a map
shouldn’t have been an issue and Thornton seems to be subject to delays at
every step of the process.  Thornton further alleges that area regional
director Erik Lund is trying to manipulate the representation on a provincially
created land use committee, in order to rig vital rezoning votes against him.

‘The whole game now is
delay me forever and let me choke on my debt,’ Thornton said.  ‘It’s just
unbelievable and staggering that they would delay due process like this.  This
is another month delay, right in prime selling season.’

…

He said the Thornton
development is being unreasonably delayed.  ‘It seems to me it’s taking an
excessive amount of time,’ he said.  Thornton agrees and says it’s the fault of
the East Sooke Director.  ‘We’ve been dealing with this since last November.  Since
Lund got elected he’s just delayed us, delayed us, delayed us,’ Thornton said.

…

Any piece of land that
they will upfront tell me they will accept, I will go and try to swap for it.  Meanwhile,
they are just delaying me while Lund continues to try and change the makeup of
the committee. He wants to rig the vote.’”

23.       The statements attributed to the
Defendant Thornton concerning the Plaintiff in paragraph 22 were made by the
Defendant Thornton and are defamatory in their natural and ordinary meaning and
the innuendos contained therein in that they mean or were understood to mean:

a.         the Plaintiff deceitfully used
or attempted to use the powers of his office to manipulate the decision-making
process relating to land use issues;

b.         the Plaintiff lied when he
stated that a new map had been produced with the latest parkland application to
the CRD board; and

c.         the Plaintiff conspired against
the Defendant Thornton and exercised his influence as a public official for the
purpose of causing anguish and economic loss for the Defendant Thornton.

[
22
]

The Defendant Thornton submits that none of his
statements in paragraph 22 are capable of bearing the meanings alleged in
paragraph 23 a and b.  I agree with the submission that the concept of deceit
or fraud does not emerge from Defendant Thornton’s statements and that there is
no implication of corruption.  There is nothing in Defendant Thornton’s
statements that suggests that the plaintiff is using his office to deliberately
cause the public to believe that he is doing something other than trying to
change the voting procedure through political conduct and tactics.  There is no
suggestion that the plaintiff is doing anything dishonestly, only that he is
attempting to restructure voting procedures so that he has more influence.  I
fail to see how any reasonable person of ordinary intelligence would understand
Defendant Thornton as saying that the plaintiff is deceitfully using the powers
of his office.

[
23
]

Similarly, I cannot find any reference to the
plaintiff lying about the production of a new map.  The only statements related
to the map are those made by the Defendant Thornton that “no new map was
submitted” and Lanny Seaton that “a map shouldn’t have been an issue”.  There
is nothing in paragraph 22 that says or suggests that the plaintiff said
anything about a map, never mind that he lied about it.  The words simply are
not there to support the meaning alleged by the plaintiff.

[
24
]

The final statements
written by the Defendant Thornton that are allegedly defamatory are contained
within paragraphs 24 and 25 of the Statement of Claim:

24.       In a circular distributed by the
Defendant Thornton throughout the lower Vancouver Island area in or about
January 2005 (“circular”), the Defendant Thornton falsely and maliciously
published of and concerning the Plaintiff the following:

“           In deciding to vote for or
against re-joining Sooke, the following information may be of importance to
you:

1.         CRD Regional Director Erik
Lund has appointed certain people who publicly favoured down-zoning rural
property to the Committee that is preparing the East Sooke ‘Official Community
Plan’ (OCP).

…

4.         All reports must be done at
the applicant’s expense, to the satisfaction of the CRD.  In this case the CRD
is really just the Director for Juan de Fuca (JDF).  That’s because Director
Lund recently seized new control over all JDF land use decisions through the
sale of a $100 vote to far-away Central Saanich.  This stripped votes from
neighbouring Sooke, Colwood and Langford – western communities that have always
protected our property rights.

With only 2 votes that
count, no Development Permit, Resolution or Bylaw can ever pass unless the
Director of the day wants it to.

Tax increases

It is frustrating when
critical decisions that affect us all can be made by just one person, without
community consultation.

…

Concentration of Power
– A Case Study

Long before he ever ran
for office Mr. Lund signed multiple submissions opposing Silver Spray.  At the
time he also argued in writing that a person with a perceived conflict of
interest must abstain from voting.  Yet once in power, he used his vote to
delay the Silver Spray parkland process almost 2 years, forcing us to sue the
CRD to finally settle it.

In pursuit of his
objectives, the Director sacrificed 10 acres of prime land suitable for a multifield
Community Sports Park by first altering the CRD Resolution to allow cash in
lieu; then by refusing to grant a sufficient extension to allow its subdivision
from a larger parcel.

As
a result:

➢

East Sooke
lost
the Sports Park,

➢

the cash-in-lieu has gone to Sooke, and

➢

the replacement value of the land has almost
doubled in value.

Obtaining land for a
Community Sports Park is a primary objective of the current East Sooke Local
Area Land Plan, yet it’s not so important to this Director.

Such examples
demonstrate that the community could be better served if one person did not
have so much power.  In my opinion, a locally elected Mayor and Council would
not have:

➢

donated $7,700 of our tax dollars to a group
(led by the person who nominated Mr. Lund for Director) that tried to block
development of another landowner’s property with a lawsuit, which failed.

➢

stripped regular funding for crossing guards to
protect our school children.

➢

wasted huge  amounts of taxpayer money in
unnecessary conflicts with Silver Spray
after
rezoning.  (Most councils
support development if in accordance with zoning to create local jobs and to
boost the tax base for the benefit of the greater community.)

By voting YES we can
put an end to this bizarre form of dictatorship.  We can all finally secure
local democracy and fiscal responsibility.”

25.       The statements contained in the
circular are defamatory in their natural and ordinary meaning and the innuendos
contained therein that they mean or were understood to mean that:

…

b.         the Plaintiff has committed a
breach of trust in his capacity of public official contrary to
section 122
of
the
Criminal Code of Canada
.

[
25
]

In my view, the circular does not suggest, imply
or mean that the plaintiff has committed a criminal act under s. 122 of the
Code.  The Defendant Thornton says that the plaintiff has made political
appointments and decisions, and reorganized the voting procedures so that he
has more control.  He does not suggest that the plaintiff has done anything
illegal and no reasonable person of ordinary intelligence would take such a
meaning from the circular.

[
26
]

In summary, Defendant
Thornton’s statements are not capable of bearing the meanings in subparagraphs
21 b and c, 23 a and b, and 25 b.  Therefore, I strike these subparagraphs from
the pleadings.

Defendant Harlow

[
27
]

The applicable paragraphs of the Statement of
Claim related to Defendant Harlow are as follows:

26.       In or about July of 2003, the
Defendant Harlow wrote to the Defendant Black Press and, or alternatively, the
Defendant Island Publishers, and on July 9, 2003, said the Defendants printed
and published in the Sooke News Mirror a letter which read as follows:

“           As a long-time advocate for
Silver Spray, and someone who feels that our area badly needs the economic
boost it will bring, I have been appalled at the constant delays orchestrated
by our regional director on the issue of parkland.  LUC ‘A’ made the right
decision to resolve this delay at the last meeting.

I am also appalled at
the last round of ‘Sooke-basking’ and the oh so transparent motive behind it.

Now it appears that out
director is attempting to remove some LUC ‘A’ members because they don’t vote
the way he wants them to.  I say they should stay because they continue to
vote based on the recommendations of our locally elected APC (grassroots
democracy at its best).

Maybe if Erik Lund had
less of a bias against Silver Spary and went into these meetings with an open
mind, he could do his job as an impartial chair and therefore would not be so
disappointed at the way a democratic decision is made.

There is no such thing
as a little democracy – we either have it or we don’t.  The alternative, any
director’s personal agenda, is scary to say the least.  Let LUC ‘A’ members to
continue to vote their conscience based on the guidelines they receive from our
elected APC and without any manipulation from what should be an ‘impartial’
chair.”

27.       The statements contained in
paragraph 26 herein are defamatory in their natural and ordinary meaning and
the innuendos contained therein in that they mean or were understood to mean
that:

a.         the Plaintiff deceitfully used
or attempted to use the powers of his office to manipulate the decision-making
process relating to land use issues;

b.         the Plaintiff is politically
corrupt;

c.         in discharging his official
duties, the Plaintiff is actuated by self-interest to the detriment of the
public that he was elected to serve;

d.         the Plaintiff conducted himself
arbitrarily and capriciously in his capacity as a public official;

e.         the Plaintiff does not conduct
himself impartially in the performance of his official duties.

[
28
]

The Defendant  Harlow submits that paragraph 26
is not capable of bearing the meanings alleged in paragraph 27 a, b, c, and d.  I
agree.

[
29
]

The Defendant Harlow writes that the plaintiff
is attempting to remove members who do not vote the way that he wants them to,
that he has a personal agenda, that he manipulates voting members, and that he
is biased against Silver Spray.  While the Defendant Harlow is clearly saying
that the plaintiff is trying to manipulate the decision-making process, there
is nothing in her writing to suggest that the plaintiff is being deceitful or
that he his politically corrupt.  She essentially disagrees with the plaintiff’s
political manoeuvring but there is no suggestion that the plaintiff is leading
the public to believe that he is doing something other than he is which is
exerting his political control and influence to alter the voting structure for
land use issues so that the Director has more power.

[
30
]

Similarly, there is nothing to suggest that the
plaintiff is actuated by self-interest.  Just because the plaintiff allegedly
attempts to remove members who do not vote the way he wants and is attempting
to change the voting structure so the director has more power, there is nothing
to suggest that the plaintiff will gain personally by this, such as securing
his position or gaining more money.  The plaintiff is essentially making
political decisions which may or may not be supported by the public.  The
office of the Director may benefit but that is a political and structural
change not a personal benefit.  The Defendant Harlow’s position is that the
consolidation of power in the hands of any director is contrary to democracy
and not good for the community, not that the Director seeks to personally
benefit from such a change.

[
31
]

Not only are Defendant Harlow’s statements
incapable of bearing the meaning that the plaintiff has conducted himself
arbitrarily and capriciously, in my view she suggests otherwise.  The Defendant
Harlow does not suggest that the plaintiff makes random choices or engages in
sudden, unaccountable changes of behaviour.  To the contrary, it is her view
that he is attempting to make systematic changes so that the Director can have
greater control in land use issues.

[
32
]

In conclusion, I find
nothing in Defendant Harlow’s statements to support the meanings alleged in
subparagraphs 27 a - d; nothing in Defendant Thornton’s statements as capable
of bearing the meanings in subparagraphs 21 b and c, 23 a and b, and 25 b; and
nothing in Defendant Wehmann’s statements support the meanings alleged in
subparagraph 17 a and c and subparagraph 19 e.  I strike subparagraphs 17 a and
c, 19 e, 21 b and c, 23 a and b, 25 b, and 27 a - d as disclosing no reasonable
claim.

Particulars of Special Damages

[
33
]

Paragraph 32 of the Statement of Claim states:

Further, the statements set out herein were
calculated to and did disparage the Plaintiff in his trade and calling and have
caused a loss of custom in the Plaintiff’s private business.

[
34
]

The Defendant Harlow sent a demand for
particulars dated August 19, 2005 requesting that in relation to paragraph 32,
the plaintiff identify his private business, the nature of the private
business, the amount of the loss, the date(s) the loss was incurred, and the
names of the customers involved.  On November 23, 2005, the plaintiff’s lawyer
responded with the name and nature of the plaintiff’s business but did not
provide further particulars on the authority of
Brown v. Cole
,
[1997] 7 W.W.R. 703 (B.C.C.A.) and
Pressler et al. v. Lethbridge et.
al
.
,
2000 BCCA 639
.  The plaintiff submits that he is not
required to provide particulars when economic losses cannot be proven.

[
35
]

In reviewing the types of compensatory damages
available in a defamation action, the B.C. Court of Appeal, in
Brown

at para.
107
, refers to possible economic damage which may result but
cannot be expressly proven.  In
Pressler
, the plaintiff had not
sought damages for business losses but the trial judge awarded damages for the
loss of pharmacy business.  The B.C. Court of Appeal upheld this decision
referring to the principle expressed in
Brown
that compensatory
damages can include possible economic damages which may result but cannot be expressly
proven (see
Pressler

at paras.
81-94
).

[
36
]

In
WeGo Kayaking Ltd. v. Sewid
,
2007
BCSC 49
, Macaulay J addresses the relationship between general and special
damages in a defamation case.  At para. 92, he explains that general economic
loss may be an independent head of general damages when a plaintiff establishes
economic loss but without sufficient precision to support a claim for special
damages.  According to Macaulay J., a claim for special damages requires more
specific proof than one for general damages.

[
37
]

Special damages must be specifically pleaded and
proven in court (
Botiuk v. Toronto Free Press Publications Ltd.
,

1995 CanLII 60 (SCC)
, [1995] 3 S.C.R. 3 at para.
109
).  In
Pootlass v. Pootlass
,

(1999)
1999 CanLII 6665 (BC SC)
, 63 B.C.L.R. (3d) 305 (B.C.S.C.), Burnyeat J. defines special damages in
the context of a defamation action.  At para. 65, he states:

Special damages
for the purposes of the law of defamation have been defined as any material or
temporal loss which is either a pecuniary loss or is capable of being estimated
in money.  Special damages are not confined to business loss or loss of
employment income.  Rather, losses such as the loss of hospitality from friends
providing such loss is capable of being estimated in money are also
recoverable.

[
38
]

When special damages are alleged, they must be
specifically set out in order to be recovered (see
Pootlass
at paras.

64
).

[
39
]

The issue is whether paragraph 32 alleges
special damages.  The plaintiff submits that his claim does not allege special
damages.  I disagree.  Although the plaintiff does not use the words “special
damages”, he does allege pecuniary loss related to his business.  As such, the
defendant must provide further particulars.

[
40
]

Pursuant to Rule 19(16), I order the plaintiff
to provide the following particulars within 10 days of the date of this
judgment: the amount of the loss, the date(s) when the
loss was incurred, the names of the customers involved and which losses were
caused by each publication complained of in the Statement of Claim.  If the
plaintiff does not provide these particulars within 10 days, paragraph 32 shall
be struck.  I note that if the plaintiff is unable to specifically plead and
prove pecuniary loss related to his business, it is still open for him to seek
compensation for such a

loss under
general damages.

“R.W. Metzger, J.”

The Honourable Mr. Justice R.W. Metzger
